Review Figma?

Reviewers see Figma as the default workspace for product design: fast to share, easy to comment on, and strong at keeping designers, developers, and stakeholders aligned in one browser-based file. People repeatedly praise real-time collaboration, prototyping, component libraries, design systems, plugins, and Dev Mode for making handoff clearer and iteration faster. Makers of LottieFiles, PaymentKit, and Slashy say it is where key product screens were designed before code. The main complaints are lag on large files, some learning curve, limited offline use, and a few pricing or admin frustrations.

results.title: Figma for Agents: Design with AI agents, connected to your design system | Product Hunt
results.content:
The problem: Every AI-generated design has the same tell: it doesn't look like your product. Components are invented. Spacing is arbitrary. The output is technically a UI, but it's nobody's design system. So designers throw it out and start over.

The solution: Skills are markdown files that encode your team's design conventions. Agents read them before touching the canvas. Combined with use\_figma, agents now have both access and context they know how to work in Figma and they know how to work in your Figma.

What you can do with it:

 🏗️ Generate component libraries from a codebase
 🔗 Sync design tokens between code and Figma variables, with drift detection
 ♿ Auto-generate screen reader specs from UI designs
 🔄 Run parallel workflows across multiple agents [...] Report

results.title: Figma Reviews (2026) | Product Hunt
results.content:
Eroan Boyer

#### What's great

Figma sits at the heart of everything we build. We run a web performance agency, and for us a design file is not a picture, it is a spec. Component libraries, spacing scales, responsive states and exact asset dimensions are all defined in Figma before a line of code is written, so developers implement what was actually intended instead of interpreting a flat mockup. That alone removes a whole class of rework. [...] Figma can slow down when files become too large or messy.

The product is powerful, but teams still need good file hygiene: clear pages, components, naming, design systems, and cleanup. Without that, even a great Figma file can become hard for developers to follow.

Developer handoff has improved a lot, but there is still room to make specs, responsive behavior, and edge states easier to understand.

#### vs Alternatives

Miro
Sketch
Canva

I choose Figma because it is easy for both designers and developers to work in the same space.

The collaboration, comments, components, prototypes, and handoff flow make it much smoother than passing static design files around. It fits well into modern product teams.

Eroan Boyer

#### What's great [...] The collaboration layer is what makes it indispensable rather than merely convenient. UX reviews happen straight in the file: a comment pinned to the exact element being discussed, in context, resolved once it is handled. It has replaced entire rounds of annotated screenshots and email threads with clients. Designers, developers and the client all work from the same source of truth, with nothing to install and no confusion about which file is the current one.

Dev Mode and the inspect panel make handoff fast, and the plugin ecosystem covers most of the remaining gaps. It is the one tool in our stack that nobody ever questions.

@leo404 You’ve landed on exactly the problem we designed for. Miora has two kinds of memory:

Personal memory lives with your account and can carry context across projects. Project memory stays inside that project, so it can hold a client’s brand rules, taboos, key decisions, and progress without bleeding into your personal work.

Skills are not limited to your own account. You can use them yourself, download and share them with teammates, or publish them to the marketplace for other creators to use.
